rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify the critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The midpoint temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.
Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one step to test whether the run can be accelerated while keeping every pair fully resolved.
Test the next shorter gradient to establish the speed limit at 40 C and measure the critical pair’s slope response. Injection 2 remains a fully resolved fallback with the maximum CRF.

Keep the gradient fixed and test higher temperature for a selectivity change that could restore resolution of the critical pair while further shortening retention. Injection 2 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Test the low-temperature endpoint at the same gradient to determine whether cooler conditions improve the critical pair without the early-peak coelution seen at 60 C. This isolates temperature-dependent selectivity before refining the gradient window.

Combine the fully resolving eight-minute gradient with an intermediate temperature to shorten retention and potentially improve the middle critical pair. At 50 C, the early and later pairs should retain more separation than at 60 C.

Trim the gradient around the observed elution window while keeping its slope close to injection 6. Starting at higher organic fraction should remove initial waiting time, with the aim of retaining full resolution in a shorter run.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step and trim the endpoint while preserving nearly the same gradient slope as injection 7. This should shorten the run further; the main check is whether the early peaks and middle critical pair remain fully resolved.

Lower the endpoint one grid step to make the gradient shallower and recover the small resolution deficit in the middle pair. The last peak previously eluted near 0.51 organic fraction, so a 0.60 endpoint should still elute all compounds comfortably.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step while holding the endpoint fixed to reduce retention with a slightly shallower gradient. Check whether the early pair remains retained and the middle pair preserves full resolution; injection 9 is the fastest fully resolved fallback.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a much steeper gradient for a faster separation on the other side of a possible middle-pair elution-order crossover. Use a moderate starting fraction and temperature to limit compression of the early pair.

Test whether cooler conditions and a higher starting organic fraction separate the middle pair in the fast-gradient regime. Lower temperature should help retain the early peaks despite the stronger starting solvent; injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Test whether a stronger starting solvent improves middle-pair selectivity, while a shallower gradient restores separation of the last pair. Keep the temperature low to counter early-peak compression, and check particularly for near-unretained peaks.

Halve the gradient slope relative to injection 13 to test whether the remaining middle-pair deficit can be recovered in a short run. Do not increase the starting organic fraction further, since the first peak is already essentially unretained.

Reduce the slope another step to seek full resolution of the middle pair, which improved slightly in injection 14. The last compound may elute during the final hold, but the previous elution window suggests a manageable retention time rather than truncation.

Return to the fastest fully resolved gradient and lower temperature one step to measure its local selectivity response. The strong-starting-solvent branch has shown diminishing resolution gains, so refine around injection 10 instead.

Test a narrower gradient window to offset the middle-pair resolution deficit while reducing initial retention. Keeping 45 C provides more early-pair separation than 50 C, which may accommodate the higher starting organic fraction.

Test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method to establish its thermal speed limit. The middle pair may improve, but the early pair is the likely constraint; retain injection 10 if it falls below full resolution.

Seek a more robust maximum-score method by lowering the starting organic fraction relative to injection 16, which should improve the marginal middle pair. At 45 C, the early pair has more selectivity margin than at 50–55 C.

Use a slope between injections 8 and 9 to seek full resolution with less retention than injection 9. The lower starting fraction should preserve more early-pair separation than injection 10, while the shallower slope than injection 8 should recover its small middle-pair deficit.

Slightly steepen the effective gradient relative to injection 10 while preserving its starting fraction and temperature. This tests whether its small resolution margin permits a further reduction in last-peak time without sacrificing the maximum CRF.

Maximum CRF is already secured, and further acceleration has repeatedly made the middle pair marginal. Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 9 for greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Raise the starting fraction one step from injection 22 to shorten retention while retaining its lower endpoint. This should offer more middle-pair resolution margin than injection 10, with the early pair checked for compression.

Lower temperature one step from injection 23 to improve early-pair separation while using the shallower gradient to protect the middle pair. This tests a nearby maximum-score method with balanced resolution margins; injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

For the final injection, combine injection 22’s shallower gradient with 45 C to seek balanced resolution margins while keeping all peaks well below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 10 remaining the fastest fully resolved method tested.
